summary: Specifies how IS-IS is extended to support Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching, including the encodings for advertising link information needed by GMPLS. It builds on the IS-IS traffic engineering extensions. It replaced RFC 4205 and has been updated by several later documents.

eli5.summary: This teaches a routing protocol to describe fancy links, such as optical fibers and time slots, not just regular data pipes, so routers can plan paths over many kinds of networks.

what is link protection type in is-is
subtitle: The new IS-IS fields that let routers advertise optical, TDM and packet links for GMPLS path planning.

tldr.problem: GMPLS controls many kinds of links, such as fibers, wavelengths and time slots, but IS-IS had no way to advertise the extra link properties that GMPLS path computation needs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds three sub-TLVs to the extended IS reachability TLV (link identifiers, link protection type and interface switching capability) and one new TLV (type 138) for shared risk link groups.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 4205, updates RFC 5305, and has itself been updated by RFC 6001, RFC 6002 and RFC 7074.

today: RFC 5307 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4205 and updates RFC 5305. It has itself been updated by RFC 6001, RFC 6002 and RFC 7074, so read those alongside it.

sections.title: What the Extensions Add
sections.content:
This RFC specifies extensions to the IS-IS routing protocol so it can carry link state information for Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS). The set of required enhancements is outlined in a separate document, RFC 4202; this one defines the encodings. Support for unnumbered interfaces assumes the Point-to-Point Three-Way Adjacency IS-IS option from RFC 5303.

The new pieces build on the sub-TLVs of the extended IS reachability TLV from RFC 5305. Three sub-TLVs are added: type 4 (Link Local/Remote Identifiers, length 8), type 20 (Link Protection Type, length 2) and type 21 (Interface Switching Capability Descriptor, variable length). One new top-level TLV is added: type 138, the GMPLS-SRLG TLV.
sections.eli5: IS-IS already lets routers share notes about their links. This RFC adds four new kinds of note for the fancy links GMPLS uses.

sections.title: Link Local and Remote Identifiers
sections.content:
The Link Local/Remote Identifiers sub-TLV (type 4) has a value of 8 octets: 4 octets of Link Local Identifier followed by 4 octets of Link Remote Identifier. If the remote identifier is unknown, it is set to 0. It is used to name links that have no IP address (unnumbered links).

This sub-TLV MUST NOT occur more than once within the extended IS reachability TLV. If it does, the receiver SHOULD ignore all of them. The identifiers are exchanged in the Extended Local Circuit ID field of the Point-to-Point Three-Way Adjacency option.
sections.eli5: If a road has no street name, each end gives it a number instead. The two ends swap numbers so they both know which road they mean.

sections.title: Link Protection Type
sections.content:
The Link Protection Type sub-TLV (type 20) is 2 octets long. The first octet is a bit vector describing the link's protection capabilities. The second octet SHOULD be set to zero by the sender and SHOULD be ignored by the receiver.

As with the identifiers sub-TLV, it MUST NOT occur more than once within the extended IS reachability TLV, and a receiver that sees it repeated SHOULD ignore all copies.
sections.eli5: This is a sticker on a road saying whether there is a spare road ready if this one gets blocked.

sections.title: Interface Switching Capability Descriptor
sections.content:
The Interface Switching Capability Descriptor (type 21) describes what an interface can switch. Its value starts with a Switching Capability octet, an Encoding octet (a value from Section 3.1.1 of RFC 3471) and 2 reserved octets. Next come eight 4-octet Maximum LSP Bandwidth fields, one for each priority from 0 to 7, in IEEE floating point format. The units are bytes (not bits) per second.

What follows depends on the switching capability. For PSC-1 to PSC-4 it is a 4-octet Minimum LSP Bandwidth plus a 2-octet Interface MTU in bytes. For TDM it is a Minimum LSP Bandwidth plus 1 octet that is 0 for Standard SONET/SDH and 1 for Arbitrary SONET/SDH. For L2SC and LSC no extra information is present. Because an interface can have more than one descriptor, this sub-TLV MAY occur more than once.
sections.eli5: This note says what kind of traffic a link can carry, how much at most, and any special details about that kind.

sections.title: The Shared Risk Link Group TLV
sections.content:
The Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG) TLV (type 138) lists groups of links that could fail together, for example because they share a physical resource. Its data is: a 6-octet System ID, 1 octet of Pseudonode Number (used if the neighbor is on a LAN interface), 1 octet of Flags, 4 octets for either the IPv4 interface address or the Link Local Identifier, 4 octets for either the IPv4 neighbor address or the Link Remote Identifier, and then a list of SRLG values of 4 octets each.

The least significant bit of the Flags octet is 1 if the interface is numbered and 0 if unnumbered; the other bits are reserved and should be 0. The TLV length is 16 + 4 * (number of SRLG values). Unlike the sub-TLVs, the SRLG TLV MAY occur more than once within the IS-IS Link State PDUs.
sections.eli5: Two roads might both cross the same bridge. This list tells everyone which roads would break together, so backup plans do not all use the same bridge.

sections.title: Graceful Restart
sections.content:
A restarting node SHOULD follow the IS-IS restart procedures (RFC 5306) and the RSVP-TE restart procedures (RFC 3473). While it does not yet know how much of its resources are really free, it SHOULD originate its Link State PDUs for TE links with 0 unreserved bandwidth and a Traffic Engineering Default metric of 0xffffff. For links whose switching capability is LSC or FSC, it SHOULD also use 0 as Max LSP Bandwidth.

Once the node has worked out its unreserved resources, taking into account LSPs preserved across the restart, it SHOULD advertise them. Before a planned restart it SHOULD advertise 0 unreserved bandwidth, which discourages new LSP setup through it. Its neighbors SHOULD keep advertising the actual unreserved bandwidth on their links toward it.
sections.eli5: A router that is rebooting puts up a sign saying 'no room right now' until it has counted what is really free, so nobody sends new traffic its way too early.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: These TLVs are not used for SPF computation or normal routing, so the extensions have no direct effect on IP routing. Tampering with them may, however, affect the underlying transport (optical and/or SONET/SDH) network. Mechanisms to secure IS-IS Link State PDUs or the TE TLVs, such as IS-IS cryptographic authentication (RFC 5304), can be used to secure the GMPLS TE TLVs as well.
sections.eli5: The notes do not change where ordinary mail goes, but a faked note could mislead the fiber network, so routers can sign their notes.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC records one new IS-IS TLV type, 138 (Shared Risk Link Group), which may appear in LSPs but not in IIH or SNP PDUs. It also records three new sub-TLV types of top-level TLV 22: type 4 (length 8), type 20 (length 2) and type 21 (variable length).
sections.eli5: The official number list gets four new entries so everyone uses the same numbers for these notes.

fields.name: Link Local Identifier
fields.desc: Identifier the sending node gives the link.

fields.name: Link Remote Identifier
fields.desc: Identifier the far end gives the link; 0 if unknown.
